title: WHOIS, Registrar, Registry, TLD, and ASN: The Ownership Layer
content:
You now understand domains and how DNS translates them to IP addresses. There is a second layer of intelligence that is equally important — the ownership layer.

Who OWNS this domain? Who OWNS this IP block? Which ORGANISATION controls this infrastructure? These questions are answered by four systems you need to know precisely: WHOIS, the registrar, the registry, and the ASN database.

---

**WHOIS: The Public Property Deed**

WHOIS is a protocol for querying the public database of internet resource ownership. When someone registers a domain, they are required to provide contact information — name, email address, phone number, organisation, and postal address. This information is stored in the WHOIS database and made publicly accessible.

Think of WHOIS as a property deed. When someone buys a house, the transaction is recorded in a public land registry — the new owner's name, the transfer date, the property address. WHOIS does the same for internet resources.

For a domain, a WHOIS record tells you:
— Who registered it (registrant name and contact — may be hidden by privacy protection)
— When it was registered (creation date — recent registration can mean a new operation, a rebrand, or a newly created threat)
— When it expires (expiry date — a domain about to expire is sometimes allowed to lapse by owners, creating takeover opportunities)
— Which company it was purchased through (registrar)
— Which nameservers are authoritative (often reveals hosting/CDN provider)

For an IP address, WHOIS tells you:
— Which organisation owns that IP block
— Which Regional Internet Registry assigned it (ARIN for North America, RIPE for Europe, APNIC for Asia Pacific)
— The organisation's contact information

**RDAP** (Registration Data Access Protocol) is the modern, structured replacement for WHOIS — it returns the same information in JSON format and is increasingly used by professional tools.

**WHOIS Privacy Protection**: Domain owners can pay a registrar to replace their registrant details in WHOIS with the registrar's privacy service address. You will see 'Domains By Proxy, LLC', 'WhoisGuard Protected', or 'Privacy service provided by Withheld for Privacy ehf'. The real owner's details are hidden. This is legal, widely used — and it is itself intelligence. An organisation using WHOIS privacy made a deliberate choice about their operational security posture.

---

**Registrar vs Registry: Two Different Things**

Almost every beginner confuses these. They sound similar. They are completely different.

**Registrar**: The company you BUY a domain from. GoDaddy, Namecheap, Cloudflare Registrar, Google Domains, Gandi, NameSilo — all registrars. They are accredited resellers. They give you a management interface, collect your payment, and submit your registration to the registry on your behalf.

Think of a registrar like an estate agent. They handle your transaction. They do not own or operate the underlying land records system.

**Registry**: The organisation that OPERATES a TLD's authoritative database. The registry is not a storefront — it is the authoritative source of truth for every registration within a TLD:
— Verisign operates .com and .net
— Public Interest Registry (PIR) operates .org
— Nominet operates .uk
— DENIC operates .de
— ICANN coordinates the global system and operates some gTLDs

Registrars submit paperwork to the registry on behalf of customers. The registry is the official land title office. Registrars are the agents who use it.

**Why does this matter?** The registrar choice can tell you something about an organisation's operational sophistication. Enterprise organisations often use premium corporate registrars with enhanced security features and multi-factor authentication on registrar accounts. Attackers setting up phishing infrastructure often use cheap registrars with minimal verification, often paired with privacy protection. When you see a client's main domain registered through a corporate registrar with no privacy protection — and a suspicious lookalike domain registered through Namecheap with privacy protection — that contrast is meaningful.

---

**TLD (Top-Level Domain): The Last Part of the Address**

The TLD is the rightmost segment: .com, .org, .net, .io, .co.uk, .gov, .edu.

**gTLD (Generic TLD)** — not tied to a specific country:
— .com — commercial, the default for global organisations
— .org — traditionally non-profits, now open to all
— .net — originally for network providers
— .io — originally British Indian Ocean Territory, now the default for tech startups
— .gov — restricted to US government entities only (CISA-verified)
— .edu — restricted to US higher education institutions only (verified)
— .mil — US military only

**ccTLD (Country Code TLD)** — assigned to specific countries:
— .uk — United Kingdom
— .de — Germany
— .in — India
— .au — Australia
— .ru — Russia

For an investigator, TLDs provide immediate context. A .gov domain means you are looking at a US government entity — which carries additional legal constraints for any engagement. A .edu domain means a US educational institution. A ccTLD tells you the target's geographic jurisdiction, which governs applicable law. A company with both .com and .io domains suggests a technology-focused operation. An organisation with only a ccTLD and no .com might be a purely domestic operation or a deliberate branding choice.

---

**ASN (Autonomous System Number): The Organisation's Complete IP Range**

This is the concept most beginners have never encountered — and the one that provides some of the most valuable intelligence in a professional engagement.

The internet is divided into Autonomous Systems — independently managed networks, each controlled by a single organisation (a company, a university, an ISP, a government agency). Each Autonomous System is assigned a globally unique number — an ASN — by IANA and the Regional Internet Registries.

Examples:
— AS13335 — Cloudflare, Inc.
— AS15169 — Google LLC
— AS16509 — Amazon (AWS)
— AS8075 — Microsoft Corporation

If an organisation operates its own internet-connected infrastructure rather than using a cloud provider entirely, they likely have their own ASN — and with it, a registered IP range.

**Why does this matter?**

When you know an organisation's ASN, you know EVERY IP address block they own — not just the ones attached to their website. This is how professionals map the complete scope of a target's internet-facing infrastructure without scanning anything.

For Meridian Financial: if they own their own servers, those servers have IP addresses within a block registered to Meridian Financial. Looking up their ASN reveals all of their IP ranges — development servers, staging environments, VPNs, mail relays, backup services. Everything.

This is achieved passively, from public registry data, using tools like bgp.he.net. No scanning required. No contact with the target's systems. The ASN database is public for the same reason WHOIS is public — network operators need to coordinate routing, abuse reporting, and incident response.

callouts.title: Key Ownership Lookup Tools
callouts.text:
who.is — User-friendly WHOIS for domains and IPs
whois.domaintools.com — Historical WHOIS, ownership change tracking
rdap.org — Modern RDAP protocol queries
bgp.he.net — ASN lookup, IP prefix discovery, BGP routing data
arin.net, ripe.net, apnic.net — Regional Internet Registry databases for IP WHOIS
mxtoolbox.com/SuperTool — All-in-one DNS and WHOIS lookup

All passive. All public. All free.

callouts.title: Historical WHOIS — Finding What Was Hidden
callouts.text: Organisations sometimes use WHOIS privacy protection now — but they may not have used it at registration. Historical WHOIS records (available through DomainTools and archived sources) sometimes reveal the real registrant from before privacy was enabled: a personal email address, a home address, or an organisation name that connects to other infrastructure. An investigator who checks both current and historical WHOIS records finds what the privacy service was meant to hide.

keyTerms.definition: A public protocol for querying domain and IP registration data. For domains: registrant, registration date, expiry, registrar, nameservers. For IPs: IP block owner and contact. The internet's property deed. May show privacy protection placeholder instead of real registrant details.

The company from which a domain is purchased and managed — GoDaddy, Namecheap, Cloudflare Registrar, Google Domains. Accredited resellers that submit registrations to the registry. The estate agent of internet real estate.

The authoritative organisation that manages all domain registrations for a specific TLD. Verisign for .com and .net. Nominet for .uk. Not a storefront — the official database that registrars submit paperwork to.

The rightmost segment of a domain (.com, .org, .uk, .gov, .edu). gTLDs are generic and unrestricted. ccTLDs are country-specific and reveal geographic jurisdiction. .gov and .edu are restricted to verified US government and educational institutions.

A unique number assigned to a network block managed by a single organisation. Every major company running its own internet infrastructure has one. Knowing a target's ASN reveals every IP address block they own — the complete map of their internet-facing infrastructure from a single public lookup.
